blocks.text: Our mission: build and care for a small compost setup

Can yesterday’s vegetable peels become useful material for growing plants? We will start a compost batch and collect evidence as it changes. Decomposers are living things that break down dead organic material.
Teacher-prepared ventilated bin and tray; dry leaves and plain cardboard; fresh uncooked plant scraps; measuring cup; stick or trowel; water bottle; gloves; label and pencil.

Use only approved inputs. No meat, dairy, oily food, plastic, animal droppings or diseased plants. Teacher cuts tough scraps and prepares holes. Cover cuts, report allergies and keep hands away from your face.
Rotate sorting, measuring, mixing and recording. Everyone completes a practical task and helps clean up. Choose an accessible role with your teacher if needed.
Plan: 10 min discuss + 40 min set up + 10 min record and clean. Add short supervised weekly checks; compost may need months.
MY START  Make a team label and read the input rules. Find the log on p. 18.
PARTNER TEST  Take turns measuring with one cup and recording the amounts.
ADULT CHECK  Wait for approved scraps, a safe bin and permission before handling. Adult checks moisture.
Separate dry leaves and plain torn cardboard (browns) from fresh vegetable peels (greens). Put rejected items aside for the teacher’s approved disposal route.
Check: no plastic, stickers or unsuitable food enters the bin.
Start with 3 loosely filled cups of browns for 1 cup of greens. This is a starting mix, not a guarantee. Keep some extra dry leaves for covering the scraps. Record the actual amounts.
Check: use the same cup size; do not pack leaves tightly.
Place a loose bed of browns in the bin. Add the measured materials and mix gently with the stick. Cover exposed peels with dry leaves; leave room for air and later mixing.
Check: do not press the mixture down or seal it airtight.
Ask the teacher to check the mixture. If dry, add a little measured water and mix. Aim for damp, not dripping. If already damp, add no water.
Check: no puddles. Teacher handles any drainage; it is not plant feed.
Write team name, start date and “Compost in progress” on the label. Close the ventilated lid and put the bin in its tray at the approved sheltered location.
Check: air holes remain open; the site is secure and away from food areas.
6 • Clean and plan the next check
Return tools, tidy the area and remove gloves. Wash hands with soap and water. Agree a weekly check date and rotate the team’s roles.
Check: observe at a distance; never sniff closely or touch mould.
MODEL ONLY • Dry leaves from school grounds | brown | 3 cups. Use your actual inputs and amounts below.
Add a little measured water and gently mix.
Wet, compacted material or unpleasant smell noticed from a distance
Tell the teacher. Add dry browns and improve airflow as directed.
Pests, heavy mould or an unsafe container
Stop handling it; the teacher checks the setup.
Check moisture and inputs, then give it time. Small bins may not heat up.
A ventilated, labelled bin on a tray with a care record. It contains a developing batch—not ready-to-use compost. Continue the diary on another sheet if needed.
Five questions • Use your own observations
1. Which item did you keep out of the bin, and why?
2. Why did we use the same cup to measure browns and greens?
3. What could happen if the mixture is pressed down or becomes too wet?
4. What changed during your checks? What evidence shows it is not yet ready for seed pots?
5. How could your family separate suitable plant scraps safely, with an adult’s help?
Explain a sorting choice using a reason.
Design a reusable label that clearly shows the start date and care reminder.
Give a one-minute report: one observation, one action and one next step.
Meet a person who does this work
With your teacher, ask a gardener or compost worker how they keep unsuitable waste out. Record one useful tip and thank them: ______________________________
Next: Soil Detectives. Our compost stays under observation while we explore soil. Use separately sourced mature compost for later planting.
MY FINISH CHECK  Tick only when your work shows it. Leave unfinished items unticked.
□ My input record names the materials and cup size.
□ My care log has real dates, observations and actions.
□ Our bin is labelled and we have agreed the next check.
IF I AM STUCK  Reread the input rules on p. 15. Brown/green describes the material type here, not just its colour.
TRY FIRST  A new compost batch is ready for seed pots: true or false?
CHECK AFTER TRYING  False. Use the separately supplied mature compost; keep observing the new batch.
Show the relevant record and explain one choice. My question or next step: __________________________
TEACHER REVIEW  The adult completes the assessment below. My own check is preparation, not permission or staff verification.
Assess the practical process as well as the record. Ask each learner to explain one action they performed.

Teacher checks the site, pest protection and moisture, and supervises adjustments. Do not use unfinished compost in seed pots or infer hygiene from warmth. For photos, obtain permission, show the setup rather than faces, and keep personal information off shared images.
Planning note: this is one activity within the wider project. Elapsed composting time is not the same as supervised learning hours.
Our mission: observe two samples and compare their drainage

Our compost needs time. While it changes, let us investigate the soil that will support our seeds. Soil contains mineral particles, organic matter, water, air and living things. Can two samples behave differently when we add water?

Two teacher-approved soil samples; two trays and spoons; hand lens; 100 mL measure; two identical plastic funnels, matching filter papers and secure supports; two graduated collecting cups; water measure; timer; labels; gloves and notebook.

Use clean, known-source samples. Avoid roadside soil, animal waste, sharp litter and dusty handling. Do not taste soil or bring it near your face. Cover cuts, report allergies and wash hands with soap after work. Keep water away from electrical devices.
Plan: 10 min prepare + 40 min investigate + 10 min record and clean. Rotate observing, measuring, timing and recording; everyone performs a practical task.
MY START  Write A and B labels. Predict one difference before touching the samples.
PARTNER TEST  One measures or pours; one times or reads. Swap roles for the next test.
ADULT CHECK  Wait for approved soil and a checked, stable test setup before pouring.
Look closely and make a fair comparison
Label the trays A and B. Record where each sample came from. Use the hand lens to compare colour, visible particles and plant pieces. Keep the samples separate.
Check: a darker colour does not prove that soil is more fertile.
Teacher prepares both samples to a similar starting moisture. Loosely fill the same measure to 100 mL for A, then B. Level gently without pressing down; clean the measure between samples.
Check: use equal volumes and the same filling method.

Secure the funnels above the collecting cups. Fit identical dry filters, then add the measured soil. Label both cups. Ask the teacher to check that each funnel is steady and its tip is clear of the cup bottom.
Check: filters, funnels and supports must match; nothing should tip over.
Measure 50 mL water. Pour it evenly over sample A in about 10 seconds. Start the timer when pouring begins. Repeat the same way for B with its own start time, or test one sample at a time.
Check: never top up one sample or press the soil during the test.
At exactly 5 minutes from each start, read collected water at eye level. Record the volume in mL, including zero if no water has collected. Note any spill or blocked filter.
Check: do not guess a result or write a number from the illustration.
If materials allow, repeat with fresh 100 mL portions and fresh matching filters. Return soil as directed by the teacher, rinse tools, wipe spills and wash hands. Keep the labels with your record.
Check: do not pour soil into the sink or drink the collected water.
MODEL ONLY • Colour: “brown, small leaf pieces”. Describe each actual sample below before explaining it.
Spill, timing change or other problem: _________________________________
What our evidence can tell us

In trial 1, sample ____ collected ____ mL more water than sample ____. If the readings are equal, write “equal”. Less collected water may mean slower drainage or more water still held in the setup. Our test cannot separate these effects or measure fertility.
Two labelled stations and a dated record. Diagram shows the arrangement, not expected water levels. Keep both sample labels for the next activity.
Five questions • Use your own results
1. What differences did you notice between A and B?
2. Which three things did you keep the same to make the test fair?
3. Which sample collected more water at five minutes? What was the difference?
4. If water spilled, how would you improve or repeat the test?
5. Why can we not decide which soil grows the best plants from this test alone?
Separate an observation from an explanation.
Draw a clear A/B comparison card with labels.
Rotate practical roles and help everyone take part.
Give a one-minute report using a measured result.
Meet a person who works with soil
Ask the school gardener how they decide when a container needs watering. Share one finding from your test and record their tip: ___________________________
Next: investigate seed germination. Keep caring for our compost; do not use unfinished compost for sowing.
MY FINISH CHECK  Tick only when your work shows it. Leave unfinished items unticked.
□ Both samples used the same soil volume, water amount and timing.
□ Each water reading has mL and any spill or timing problem is noted.
□ My comparison uses my numbers, not the picture.
IF I AM STUCK  For a difference, subtract the smaller collected volume from the larger. Look back at the two recorded readings.
TRY FIRST  A darker soil sample must be more fertile: true or false?
CHECK AFTER TRYING  False. Colour alone does not establish fertility, and this test compares collected water.
Show the relevant record and explain one choice. My question or next step: __________________________
TEACHER REVIEW  The adult completes the assessment below. My own check is preparation, not permission or staff verification.
Observe the process as well as the written record
This activity develops practical inquiry; it is not a laboratory soil-quality test.

Provide large-print labels, stable supports and an accessible work height. Pair learners for pouring or reading when needed; each learner still completes a suitable practical action. Teacher supplies safe samples and checks the setup before pouring.
If photographing evidence, show the apparatus and record rather than faces. Obtain permission, omit personal details and use only teacher-approved sharing. A paper drawing is equally acceptable.
Allow about one hour for this guided activity within the project timetable.
Our mission: follow 10 seeds as they begin to grow

We have explored soil. Now we will watch seeds start growing on damp paper, where the first root is easy to see. Germination is the start of a seed’s growth. Water, air and a suitable temperature help it begin; follow the guidance for your chosen seed.
Classroom illustration. Our investigation uses exactly 10 seeds, shown in the setup diagrams.

10 intact, untreated seeds of one type from one batch; clean shallow tray; plain absorbent paper; clean water and dropper; labels; pencil; hand lens; daily record. Teacher may provide a loose cover suitable for the chosen seed.

Teacher checks seed suitability and allergies. Never eat test seeds or sprouts. Keep seeds away from mouths, wash hands after handling and tell the teacher about mould. Do not sniff or touch mouldy material.
Plan: one guided setup lesson, then brief daily checks until the agreed end date. Rotate counting, moistening, observing and recording so everyone practises.
MY START  Prepare a 1–10 seed-position map. Leave space for the date and seed type.
PARTNER TEST  Count each position once, then ask your partner to check the total.
ADULT CHECK  Wait for approved seeds, a safe location and an agreed care routine. Report mould.
Read the seed packet with your teacher. Record the seed type and batch or source. Count 10 intact untreated seeds. Agree the location and final observation date using the packet guidance.
Check: keep the original total at 10; do not replace a seed after starting.
Line the clean tray with plain absorbent paper. Add clean water a little at a time until the paper is evenly damp. Ask the teacher to remove any puddle.
Check: seeds need air too; do not submerge them in water.
Place the 10 seeds apart in two rows of five. Copy positions 1–10 onto a paper map beside the tray. Label the tray with team, seed type and start date.
Check: keep the numbering on your map; do not write on the seeds.
Count a seed as germinated when its first root is visible. A swollen seed without a visible root is not counted yet. Mark each germinated seed’s position on your map.
Check: do not pull a seed off the paper to inspect its root.
Check at about the same time daily. Record new seeds with roots today and the total so far. Add only enough water to keep paper damp, and note the care action.
Check: the total cannot exceed 10. Count each seed only once.
Keep the tray in the teacher-approved location. Follow seed guidance for temperature and light; use a loose cover only if directed. Plan who checks it between lessons.
Check: teacher handles mould or disposal. Record removed or missing seeds; never silently replace them.
MODEL ONLY • Yesterday 3; new today 2; total so far 5. Complete the table with your own daily counts.

Continue on a dated sheet if the selected seed needs longer. Total so far = yesterday’s total + new today. If a seed is removed after germinating, keep its earlier germination in the total and note its removal.
Germinated seeds ÷ 10 × 100 = germination percentage Our result: ____ ÷ 10 × 100 = ____% Example only: 8 ÷ 10 × 100 = 80%. Keep all 10 original seeds in the denominator.
Missing or removed seeds and reason: ______________________________
A labelled tray, ten mapped seeds and a daily care record. This picture shows the setup; roots appear later if conditions and seeds are suitable.
1. What change told you that a seed had germinated?
2. Why did we keep the paper damp without covering the seeds in water?
3. How did your seed map prevent double-counting?
4. What was your final percentage? Does a seed that has not germinated yet have to be dead?
5. What would you check or improve if you repeated the investigation?
Explain a result without assuming every ungerminated seed is dead.
Design a clear seed map and care reminder.
Rotate practical roles and arrange daily care.
Present the count, percentage and one limitation.
Meet a person who grows seedlings
Ask a gardener or nursery worker why they check seeds before sowing many trays. Record one tip and thank them: ______________________________
Next: set up a fair growth comparison. Use the planting method agreed in Activity 4. Do not pull fragile seedlings from paper or mix unequal seedlings into a fair test.
MY FINISH CHECK  Tick only when your work shows it. Leave unfinished items unticked.
□ My ten positions match the original ten seeds.
□ New today and total so far are different entries; the total never exceeds ten.
□ My final percentage uses all ten original seeds.
IF I AM STUCK  Yesterday 3 seeds had roots; today 2 more do. The total is 3 + 2 = 5, not 2. Use your own counts.
TRY FIRST  A swollen seed with no visible root counts as germinated here: true or false?
CHECK AFTER TRYING  False. This investigation counts a seed only when its first root is visible.
Show the relevant record and explain one choice. My question or next step: __________________________
TEACHER REVIEW  The adult completes the assessment below. My own check is preparation, not permission or staff verification.
Check practical skills, care and honest evidence
This small classroom test uses visible root emergence; it is not an official seed-certification test.

Provide a large-print numbered map, stable tray and accessible work height. Let learners point, dictate or draw observations as needed while ensuring each carries out a suitable practical task. Use a magnifier without holding it in direct sunlight.

Agree the observation period for the chosen seed and organise care across school closures. A missing seed creates uncertainty: retain the denominator, note the loss and avoid over-interpreting the percentage. Arrange safe disposal or suitable planting after the test.
For evidence photos, obtain permission, focus on the tray and omit personal details. Paper drawings work equally well. Daily elapsed time is not the same as supervised learning hours.
Activity 4 • Set Up a Fair Growth Comparison
Our mission: compare a base growing medium with a compost mix

Will adding mature compost change seedling growth? We will prepare two groups of pots and observe what actually happens. A growing medium is the material around a plant’s roots. Three pots in each group help us notice differences between individual plants.

Six identical pots with drainage holes and separate saucers; one batch of teacher-approved base medium; mature compost; measuring cup; two mixing trays; spoon; six untreated seeds from one batch; labels; water measure; ruler and notebook.

Teacher checks compost maturity and suitability. Do not use unfinished compost from Activity 1. Teacher prepares drainage holes. Avoid dust, cover cuts, keep hands away from your face and wash with soap after handling materials. Do not eat the seeds.
Plan: one guided setup lesson followed by scheduled care and measurements. Rotate measuring, mixing, sowing and recording so every learner practises.
MY START  Write six labels: A1, A2, A3, B1, B2, B3. Read the plan on p. 36.
PARTNER TEST  Explain the one planned difference; check equal pot volumes and labels together.
ADULT CHECK  Wait for approved compost, seed depth, watering rule and prepared drainage holes.
A: measure 4 cups of base medium. B: mix 3 cups of the same base medium with 1 cup of mature compost. Use the same cup and loose filling method. Make more batches in the same proportions if needed.
Check: this 25% compost example needs teacher approval for your seed and materials.
Label pots A1, A2, A3 and B1, B2, B3. Put an equal measured final volume in every pot, leaving watering space below the rim. Keep A and B mixing tools separate or clean them between groups.
Check: matching pots, drainage holes, fill volume and gentle settling; do not compress one mix more.
Use fresh seeds of the same type and batch, not the seedlings on paper. Make one hole per pot at the packet depth. Sow one seed, cover gently and record the common sowing date.
Check: no extra seeds or fertiliser. Keep the label fixed to each pot.
Care fairly and start the record

Ask the teacher to demonstrate the moisture check and agree when to water. Apply the same rule to every pot. Add water gently in measured amounts only when needed; record the actual amount for each pot.
Check: never leave pots standing in water. Different water amounts must be recorded as a limitation.

Put all six pots in the same suitable growing area. Alternate A and B as shown. On agreed days, shift each pot one place along the row, moving the end pot to the first place. Keep labels attached and record the move.
Check: equal access to light; avoid a position that shades another pot.

Record medium, seed and sowing date for every pot. Agree daily checks and who will care for the pots between lessons. Note the date each shoot first appears above the medium. Return tools, wipe spills and wash hands.
Check: record non-emergence or damage. Do not secretly replace a failed seed.
Start with the printed changed factor below. Fill the other rows from your approved method, not a guessed result.
Medium composition: A base; B compost mix
Prediction: I think __________________ because __________________. Water added: record date, pot ID and mL on the Activity 5 care sheet.
Six labelled, sown pots ready for care—not six grown plants yet. Keep this position map with your records. Draw an arrow showing where the main light comes from.
1. What is the one planned difference between groups A and B?
2. Which three things must stay the same for a useful comparison?
3. Why do we use three pots per group instead of only one?
4. How will we record a pot that needs extra water or fails to produce a shoot?
5. Would taller plants alone prove that compost nutrients caused the difference? Why?
Identify another factor that could affect growth.
Design durable labels and a clear care rota.
Share measuring, sowing, watering and cleaning duties.
Explain the plan to another team before starting.
Meet a gardener or nursery worker
Ask how they choose a suitable compost mix and avoid overwatering. Record one useful tip: __________________________________________
Next: measure, interpret and share. Follow each pot separately in Activity 5. We are comparing whole growing mixes, not isolating a nutrient effect.
MY FINISH CHECK  Tick only when your work shows it. Leave unfinished items unticked.
□ My plan states the changed factor and at least three things kept alike.
□ All six pots have the correct label and a recorded sowing date.
□ The watering rule, care roles and next check are agreed.
IF I AM STUCK  Group A has base medium; B has a compost mix. Keep pot size, seed batch and sowing method alike.
TRY FIRST  A failed seed should be secretly replaced to make the display look complete: true or false?
CHECK AFTER TRYING  False. Record the failure. If the teacher restarts a pot, label a new trial and retain the first record.
Show the relevant record and explain one choice. My question or next step: __________________________
TEACHER REVIEW  The adult completes the assessment below. My own check is preparation, not permission or staff verification.
Assess the process and evidence; do not award higher marks simply because one group grows taller.

Approve the seed, pot size, base medium, compost source and mixing proportion. Demonstrate a safe moisture check and set the observation period. Provide an accessible work height, large labels and measuring support. Each learner performs a suitable practical action.

Different mixes affect moisture, air spaces and nutrients together. Watering to a common moisture rule may require different volumes; document these and avoid claiming a nutrient-only effect. If restarting a failed pot, label it as a new trial and keep the original record.
Digital citizenship: obtain permission for photos, show the setup and omit personal details. A drawing is equally acceptable.
Our mission: explain our growth comparison using evidence

Our six pots are ready. Now we will care for them, measure each seedling and compare groups A and B. A useful result can be a difference, a similarity or an unexpected outcome. We must report what happened, not what we hoped would happen.
Classroom illustration only. Your plants may look different; use your own measurements.
The six labelled pots from Activity 4; ruler marked in centimetres; pencil; growth and care records; water measure; graph sheet; optional teacher-approved camera.
Keep pots stable and handle them from the base. Do not pull, stretch or bend seedlings. Wipe spills and wash hands after handling soil. Teacher handles mould, pests and damaged pots.
Plan regular readings on the same days after sowing. Rotate measuring, checking, recording and care duties. Each student measures a plant and explains a result.
MY START  Find the pot labels and your last dated record. Prepare the next reading table.
PARTNER TEST  Read the ruler, then swap so both learners measure and check a pot ID.
ADULT CHECK  Ask for the first true-leaf demonstration and agreed care routine; report unsafe pots or mould.
Keep the method the same for every pot
Read the pot ID before touching the record. Write the date and days since sowing. Check all pots at about the same time. Record emergence dates so you can notice differences in seedling age.

Hold the ruler vertically beside the plant. Align the zero mark with the medium surface, not the bottom of the pot. Read the height level with the shoot tip in cm. Do not straighten the plant by pulling it.
Check: the drawing shows a 10 cm example; it is not a result to copy.
With the teacher, identify true leaves and count them separately from seed leaves. Record colour, wilting or damage without picking leaves. Ask a teammate to check the pot ID and reading.
Our ruler’s smallest division: ______ cm. If marks are 1 mm apart, that is 0.1 cm. Use only the precision your ruler supports.
Use the same routine at every reading
Write NE, not a height of zero.
Write NM and explain the reason.
Write D and the date; retain earlier records.
Continue the Activity 4 moisture rule. Record water in mL for each pot, any position change and any unusual event. Keep the original record if a pot fails; do not replace it silently.

For each date, add the heights of living seedlings actually measured in group A. Divide by the number measured, called n. Do the same for B. Report n beside every mean. If n = 0, write “no mean”; do not divide by zero.
Choose one date. Present the two means, n values, emergence and visible condition. State one limitation and one improvement. Share speaking roles and point to the original records.
Check: height alone does not prove healthier growth, and this small test cannot prove that compost always helps.
Agree who will keep caring for the plants. Return tools and use the school’s approved route for pots and growing material. Do not abandon living plants after the presentation.
Write the date first. MODEL ONLY • A1 | 7 cm | 2 true leaves | upright. Use your own observations below.
Team: ______ Date: ______ Days after sowing: ____ Ruler precision: ____ cm
Second reading: date ______ Days after sowing ____
Use dated copies for additional readings and daily care. Keep NE, NM and D visible; never turn missing readings into zero-height plants.
Compare the same dates and show how many were measured

1. Write a title. Label days after sowing across the bottom and mean height in cm up the side. 2. Choose equal intervals that fit your largest result; write the scale values. 3. Plot one date first. Match its day and height to the two axes; check it with a partner. 4. Plot the rest. Use different A/B symbols and a key. Join consecutive available readings; leave gaps for missing means.
If there is only one reading date, show two labelled points or bars instead of claiming a trend over time. Keep n in the table beside the graph.
Finished outcome: labelled plants, dated records, a graph and an explanation. This is an illustrative view, not an expected growth result.
On day ____, group ____ had a mean height of ____ cm (n = ____), compared with ____ cm (n = ____) for group ____.
To check the result more carefully, we would _______________________. Our plant-care owner and next check date: __________________________
Five questions • Refer to your records
1. Why must the ruler’s zero mark start at the medium surface?
2. How did you handle a missing reading or a seed that did not emerge?
3. What do the mean and n tell us together?
4. What other observations help us interpret plant height?
5. What can your results support, and what would you investigate next?
Check whether the conclusion matches the evidence.
Design a clear display with labels and a graph key.
Share measurement, care and speaking roles.
Present one dated result, one limitation and one next step.
Share with a person who grows plants
Show your findings to the school gardener or a nursery worker with teacher support. Ask what they would check next. Record their suggestion: __________________
Continue to the skill portfolio and showcase pages. Include evidence from composting, soil study, germination and the growth comparison.
MY FINISH CHECK  Tick only when your work shows it. Leave unfinished items unticked.
□ Each measurement has its pot ID, date and cm unit.
□ My mean includes only living seedlings actually measured; I report n.
□ My graph has labels and a key, and my claim includes a limitation.
IF I AM STUCK  Use the worked means on p. 41. Add the measured heights, divide by the number measured and write that number as n.
TRY FIRST  An unmeasured plant should be entered as 0 cm: true or false?
CHECK AFTER TRYING  False. Use NM and give the reason. NE means no emergence and D means died; neither is a made-up height.
Show the relevant record and explain one choice. My question or next step: __________________________
TEACHER REVIEW  The adult completes the assessment below. My own check is preparation, not permission or staff verification.
Reward careful process and honest interpretation
Correct units, codes, means and n

Demonstrate true leaves versus seed leaves using the selected crop. Fix a measurement schedule and check ruler precision. Compare living measured seedlings while also reporting emergence, deaths and missing readings. Changes in n can change the mean; do not treat it as growth of the same plants without checking individual records.
Provide large-print records, accessible pot positions and partner support. Each learner completes a suitable practical task and explains evidence orally, in writing or through an annotated drawing.
Photos need permission; omit faces and personal details where possible. Use teacher-approved sharing.

activities.title: Activity 4 • Set Up a Fair Growth Comparison
